correctness.rationale: At first firing, each chip count is at least vertex degree minus earlier-fired neighbors. Summing at total chip mass equal to the number of edges forces no adjacent same-round firings and equality at every vertex; hence chip allocation is uniquely determined by the surjective firing phase map. The predecessor-neighbor condition is necessary and sufficient to avoid premature or repeated firing. For complete multipartite graphs each round lies in one part, neighboring rounds have different parts, and surjections to ordered rounds are counted by products ordered-block Stirling factors. Sharp period support follows from circular separation and Dirac Hamiltonicity for a feasible integer quota vector. All quantifiers at least three parts, positive part sizes and all T are handled. Explicit full-state enumeration of 20,814 allocations on nine graphs agrees with independent word/Stirling enumerations; finite tests are not the infinite proof.

originality.rationale: The complete c-partite construction in Jiang (2010) establishes possible periods and supplies a single five-cycle example on \(K_{2,2,1}\), but not a labelled count of all such critical-mass single-pass configurations. The new claim gives 40 states/eight orbits there, an all-T Stirling-weighted census, and an exact gapless sharp period interval for every at least three parts. Scully–Jiang–Zhang study admissible vertex firing patterns rather than this chip-allocation census. The source-reversal relationship is older and is not claimed new. A plausible 2000 source-reversal paper was not accessible in full; that is recorded as a priority risk rather than pronounced non-covering. value.rationale: The exact number of recurrent chip configurations is a natural invariant beyond the existence of periods, and the primary paper singles out a five-period complete-tripartite example without enumerating its whole sector. The new results give all periods and the exact count of configurations and orbits for arbitrary part sizes, plus a sharp dependence on the largest part. Unlike the two-part prior formula, the at least three parts problem has odd periods and proper cyclic multicolour words. The theorem makes no claim to all periodic or transient states.
